3270:
A conflict is a serious clash or struggle between two or more sides that want different things, believe different things, or cannot coexist peacefully. The two sides are in direct opposition — meaning what one side wants, needs, or stands for is incompatible with what the other side wants, needs, or stands for.

Think of it this way: when two forces push against each other, neither letting the other through — that push and resistance is the essence of conflict.
What Makes Something a "Conflict" (and Not Just a Disagreement)?

Not every difference of opinion is a conflict. If you and a friend can't agree on what movie to watch, that's just a mild disagreement. A conflict is bigger. It carries:

  • Seriousness — the stakes matter to those involved.
  • Opposition — the two sides are genuinely at odds, not just slightly different.
  • Tension or struggle — there is active friction, not just a passive difference.

A conflict can be short or long, quiet or loud, internal or external — but it always involves this fundamental clash.
The Full Spectrum — From Mild to Extreme

One of the most important things to understand about "conflict" is that it covers a wide range of intensity. It does NOT always mean physical fighting.

  • At its mildest: A conflict can be a deep, ongoing disagreement between two people about values, money, or responsibilities — no shouting, no violence, just persistent opposition.
  • In the middle: A conflict can be a prolonged dispute between organizations, communities, or political parties — with debates, protests, legal battles, and power struggles.
  • At its most intense: A conflict can mean war — armed fighting between nations or groups.

The word "conflict" comfortably describes all of these. Context tells you where on the spectrum a particular conflict falls.

1. Conflict Between People (Interpersonal Conflict)

This is a clash between two or more individuals. It could be between family members, colleagues, neighbors, or strangers.

There was a long-running conflict between the two brothers over their father's property.

2. Conflict Between Groups or Nations

This is a clash between larger forces — communities, political parties, ethnic groups, or countries. When it involves military action, it is often called an armed conflict (a formal, careful way of saying "war" without necessarily using that word).

The armed conflict between the two neighboring countries lasted nearly a decade.

3. Internal Conflict (Within a Person)

This is one of the richest uses of the word. An internal conflict is a struggle happening inside a single person's mind — between two opposing feelings, desires, duties, or beliefs.

She felt a deep internal conflict — she wanted to speak the truth, but she was afraid of the consequences.

This is not a clash with another person. It is a clash within oneself. Two parts of you want opposing things, and you are torn.

4. Conflict of Interest

This is a specific, very common phrase. It refers to a situation where a person's personal interests clash with their professional duty or responsibility.

The judge had to step down from the case because of a conflict of interest — the accused was his close friend.

Here, the judge's personal loyalty (to his friend) conflicts with his professional duty (to be impartial). The two cannot coexist, so one must give way.

5. Conflict Between Ideas, Values, or Principles

Sometimes the clash is not between people at all, but between abstract things — beliefs, values, laws, or goals.

There is a constant conflict between the desire for freedom and the need for security in any society.

At the heart of every conflict is incompatibility — two things that cannot both be true, satisfied, or victorious at the same time.

  • Two countries both claim the same territory. Both claims cannot be fully honored. → Conflict.
  • A person wants to be honest AND wants to protect someone they love from painful truth. Both cannot be fully achieved. → Internal conflict.
  • A company's goal to maximize profit conflicts with its employees' demand for better pay. Both cannot be fully satisfied simultaneously. → Conflict.

This is what makes a conflict a conflict. It is not just that two things are different — it is that they are mutually blocking each other.

These are the most natural phrases built around this word, and understanding them sharpens your grasp of the noun.

  • "In conflict with" means actively opposing or clashing with something/someone.

    His actions were in direct conflict with the company's values.

  • "Come into conflict" means to begin clashing — the moment opposition starts.

    The two leaders came into conflict over how to handle the crisis.

You will also often see this phrase. Conflict resolution is the process of ending or managing a conflict — finding a way for the opposing sides to reduce tension, compromise, or reach an agreement. It is an entire field of study in diplomacy, psychology, and management.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Conflict" is not a neutral, cold word. It carries weight. When you say there is a conflict, you are signaling that the situation is serious, that real interests are at stake, and that some kind of outcome — resolution, victory, defeat, or compromise — is still uncertain.

It is stronger than "disagreement," "difference," or "dispute" in most contexts, though those words can sometimes be used similarly. "Conflict" usually implies the tension is deep-rooted, significant, and not easily dismissed.

A conflict (noun) is a serious clash or struggle between opposing sides — whether those sides are people, groups, nations, ideas, values, or even parts of a single person's mind. The core of every conflict is incompatibility: two forces pushing against each other because both cannot fully win or coexist at the same time. It ranges from internal emotional struggles to full-scale war, and it always signals that something real and significant is at stake.
3271:
When two things conflict, they are directly opposed to each other in a way that makes it impossible — or very difficult — for both to be true, happen, or exist at the same time without causing a problem.

Think of it like two people trying to walk through a narrow doorway at the exact same moment. They run right into each other. Neither can move forward freely. That collision — that incompatibility — is the feeling "conflict" captures as a verb.
How It Works in a Sentence

As a verb, "conflict" almost always follows this pattern:

[Thing A] conflicts with [Thing B]

The word "with" is almost always attached. You rarely say "A conflicts B." You say "A conflicts with B." This is one of the most important things to remember about using this word correctly.
What Kinds of Things Can Conflict?

1. Facts, Statements, or Information

When two pieces of information say opposite things, they conflict — because you cannot accept both as true at the same time.

  • "The suspect's alibi conflicts with the security camera footage." The suspect claims to have been somewhere else, but the camera proves otherwise. Both cannot be right simultaneously.
  • "These two studies conflict — one concludes that coffee is beneficial, the other that it is harmful."

2. Schedules or Events

When two events are planned for the same time and you can only be in one place, they conflict.

  • "My job interview conflicts with my cousin's wedding. I can't attend both."
  • "The team meeting conflicts with the training session."

Nothing is "wrong" with either event by itself — the problem is purely that they occupy the same slot, making both impossible to honour.

3. Interests, Goals, or Desires

When what one person (or group) wants directly stands in the way of what another person (or group) wants.

  • "Her goal of saving money conflicts with her husband's desire to travel every year."
  • "The company's interest in cutting costs conflicts with the employees' demand for higher salaries."

Both goals may be perfectly reasonable on their own — the conflict arises because satisfying one makes it harder (or impossible) to satisfy the other.

4. Rules, Laws, or Principles

When two rules or laws point you in opposite directions and you cannot follow both.

  • "This new company policy conflicts with federal law — the business cannot enforce both."
  • "His commitment to honesty conflicts with his manager's instruction to withhold information from clients."

5. A Person's Own Feelings or Thoughts

Sometimes your own inner emotions or desires can conflict — when one part of you pulls in one direction and another part pulls in the opposite direction.

  • "Her feelings conflict — she loves her hometown deeply, yet she desperately wants to leave it."

When this internal tension is the focus, the phrase "feel conflicted" (discussed below) is even more natural.

This is perhaps the most important nuance to understand, and many learners miss it.

Two things can simply be different without conflicting. A red car and a blue car are different, but they don't conflict. Two people can prefer different foods — one loves pasta, the other loves sushi — and there is no conflict. Both preferences can exist comfortably side by side.

Conflict requires incompatibility. It means that when one thing is accepted or pursued, it creates a direct problem for the other.

  • "She prefers tea; he prefers coffee." → Just different. No conflict.
  • "She says she was home all night. Her phone's location data shows she was across town." → A genuine conflict. Both cannot be true. One must be wrong.

The moment you feel that "both can't be right" or "both can't happen," that's when the word "conflict" becomes the right choice.
The Forms You'll Encounter Most Often

Conflicting (adjective) — One of the most common ways this word appears. It describes two or more things that oppose each other.

  • "The investigation turned up conflicting evidence." (Some evidence points one way, other evidence points another — they are in opposition.)
  • "There are conflicting reports about what caused the explosion." (Different sources are saying different things; they can't all be correct.)
  • "She experienced conflicting emotions after hearing the news — relief, but also sadness." (Two opposite feelings existing at the same time inside her.)

Conflicted (adjective) — Used specifically to describe a person who is torn between two opposing feelings, choices, or loyalties. The opposition is happening inside them.

  • "He felt conflicted about accepting the promotion — it was a brilliant opportunity, but it meant moving far away from his family."
  • "She was conflicted — she wanted to tell the truth, but she also didn't want to hurt her friend."

The key distinction: things (facts, schedules, rules) conflict with each other, while a person who is inwardly torn feels conflicted.

Clash — Very close in meaning, but carries a slightly more intense, dramatic, or emotional charge. A clash suggests a forceful, direct collision — often between people or personalities.

  • "Their personalities clash terribly." (Strong, emotional, personal)
  • "Their schedules conflict." (Neutral, factual, about logistics)

You can often swap the two, but "conflict" tends to sound more measured and formal, while "clash" sounds more heated.

Contradict — This is specifically about statements or claims saying the opposite of each other. If you contradict someone, you say something that directly opposes what they said. "Conflict" is broader — it applies to schedules, interests, laws, and feelings, not just spoken or written statements. You would not say "my Tuesday appointment contradicts my Wednesday meeting" — but you would say they conflict.

Disagree — This is used specifically for people holding different opinions. Objects, events, and rules don't "disagree." But they absolutely can "conflict." A scheduling app would never tell you that your meetings "disagree" — but it would rightly tell you they conflict.

To conflict (verb) means to be in direct opposition to something else — in a way where both things cannot comfortably or logically coexist, both cannot be true at the same time, or both cannot happen at the same time.

Use it when:

  • Two facts or stories cannot both be true
  • Two events are scheduled at the same time and both cannot be attended
  • Two goals or needs pull in opposite directions
  • Two rules or laws cannot both be obeyed
  • (And for internal emotional tension, "feel conflicted" is the natural phrase)

The word always implies incompatibility — not just difference, but actual opposition where one thing gets in the way of the other. That's the heart of it.
3272: Confluence means the coming together of two or more things into a single point or place. Think of it as a meeting — but a very specific kind. In a confluence, things don't just cross paths and go their separate ways. They flow toward each other, and where they meet, they combine into something bigger and unified.

The most concrete image of confluence is geographical. When two rivers flow toward each other and join, that meeting point — and the act of their joining — is called a confluence. The rivers were separate. Now they become one. The water mingles together and flows forward as a single, larger stream.

A real-world example: the confluence of the Missouri River and the Mississippi River near St. Louis, USA, where both rivers merge into one powerful flow.
The figurative meaning — and this is where the word truly shines

Confluence is used far more often in a non-literal, figurative sense. It describes any situation where multiple forces, ideas, events, or circumstances come together at the same time or place — and their coming together produces something significant.

Consider these scenarios:

  • A startup succeeds because of a confluence of factors: a great product, perfect timing, skilled founders, and investor interest — all arriving at once.
  • A scientific breakthrough emerges from a confluence of ideas — theories from biology, chemistry, and physics flowing into one new discovery.
  • A political movement rises from a confluence of public frustration, economic hardship, and a charismatic leader all converging at the right moment.

In every case, the key idea is the same: separate things flowing together, combining, and creating something more significant than any one of them alone.
What exactly does confluence refer to?

As a noun, confluence can point to two closely related things:

1. The place or point where things come together.
"The city was built at the confluence of two rivers."

2. The event or act of things coming together.
"Her success was the result of a confluence of talent and opportunity."

Both are equally correct and common.
The feeling and weight of the word

Confluence is not a cold, neutral word. It carries a sense that the coming-together is meaningful — that the meeting of these things matters and that the result is greater, or more interesting, than any single element on its own.

When a writer or speaker chooses "confluence," they are signaling that the combination feels almost natural and organic — like rivers that were always destined to flow toward each other. It elevates the description. Instead of flatly saying "several things combined," saying "a confluence of factors" suggests an inevitable, flowing, purposeful convergence.
How confluence differs from similar words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

Convergence — emphasizes things moving toward a point, whereas confluence emphasizes the actual meeting and merging at that point. Convergence is about the journey; confluence is about where things arrive and combine.

Intersection — a crossing point where things meet but don't necessarily merge. Think of two roads crossing; each road continues on its own path. Confluence implies a deeper, more lasting coming-together where the things actually blend.

Junction — the physical point where things meet, usually roads or railway lines. It's more mechanical and narrow; confluence has far greater depth and works beautifully for abstract ideas, not just physical places.

Merger — suggests a complete, often formal blending (like two companies). Confluence is more organic and can describe even temporary or partial coming-together.

So confluence occupies a special space: it describes a meeting that feels fluid and natural — like rivers — where the coming-together creates something unified and meaningful.

Literal (geographical):

  • "The ancient city was founded at the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers."
  • "The two mountain streams rushed toward their confluence at the valley floor."

Figurative:

  • "Her remarkable career was the product of a confluence of hard work, raw talent, and exceptional mentorship."
  • "The 1960s witnessed a stunning confluence of social movements that permanently reshaped history."
  • "The film resonated with millions because of a rare confluence of a powerful script, brilliant performances, and perfect timing."
  • "The disaster was caused by a deadly confluence of poor planning, bad weather, and equipment failure."
  • "At the confluence of Eastern and Western philosophy, an entirely new way of thinking was born."

Confluence = the flowing together of two or more things — whether rivers, ideas, events, forces, or circumstances — into a single, unified meeting point, with the implication that the coming-together is meaningful and that the result is larger than any single part alone.
3273:
To conform means to adjust yourself, your behavior, or something else so that it matches, fits, or agrees with a rule, standard, pattern, or expectation.

Think of it like a mold. When liquid is poured into a mold, it takes the mold's shape — it conforms to it. That's the heart of the word: something changes or adjusts itself to fit what is required or expected.

1. Social/Behavioral Conforming

This is the most common use. It means to behave the way a group, society, authority, or set of rules expects you to behave.

  • A new employee conforms to the company's dress code by wearing formal clothes.
  • A student conforms to classroom rules by raising their hand before speaking.
  • A teenager conforms to peer pressure by wearing the same brands as their friends.

Notice: the person changes or adjusts their behavior to match what is expected around them.

2. Physical/Technical Conforming

Here, a thing matches or fits a required shape, pattern, or specification.

  • The building must conform to safety regulations.
  • The product conforms to international quality standards.
  • The new road design conforms to the natural shape of the landscape.

"Conform" is almost always followed by "to" or "with." Both are correct, but conform to is more common.

  • She refused to conform to society's expectations.
  • The experiment's results conform with the original theory.

"Conform" carries a subtle but important feeling: there is some external pressure, expectation, or standard already in place, and the subject (a person or thing) is either matching it or being asked to match it.

This is why the word is frequently used in contexts involving:

  • Social pressure — peer groups, culture, society
  • Authority — laws, governments, institutions
  • Rules and standards — regulations, specifications, religious doctrines

A person can conform willingly or unwillingly — the word itself doesn't specify which. Context tells you.

  • He chose to conform to the new rules because he believed in them. (willing)
  • She felt forced to conform to social norms, even though she disagreed. (unwilling)

This is an important nuance. Conforming is not always a sign of weakness or blind obedience. Sometimes it is simply practical, respectful, or wise. And sometimes it reflects genuine agreement.

The word "conform" is neutral by itself, but it picks up positive or negative meaning from context.

Positive or neutral: Conforming to safety standards, conforming to professional norms, conforming to laws — these are generally seen as responsible and good.

Negative: When used in a social or personal context, "conform" often carries a slightly critical or sad undertone, suggesting that someone is suppressing their individuality or blindly following the crowd.

  • "She gave up her dreams just to conform." — clearly negative
  • "The bridge was built to conform to modern safety codes." — clearly positive/neutral

It's easy to confuse "conform" with similar words. Here's how it's different:

  • Obey = follow an instruction or command from an authority. It's about a direct command. You obey a person or an order. You conform to a standard or norm — which can be unspoken and social, not necessarily a direct command.
  • Comply = act in accordance with a request or requirement, often in a formal or legal sense. Comply is more about a specific, often short-term requirement. Conform is broader and often ongoing — it's about consistently matching a standard or norm over time.
  • Adapt = change yourself to work better in a new situation. Adapting is about surviving or functioning well in new circumstances. Conforming is specifically about matching what is expected or required by others or by a standard.

Knowing the family of a word helps you understand and use it more flexibly.

  • Conformity (noun) — the state of conforming; following accepted rules or standards. "There was great pressure for conformity in that school."
  • Conformist (noun/adjective) — a person who tends to conform to social norms. "He was a conformist who never questioned the rules."
  • Nonconformist (noun/adjective) — a person who refuses to conform to accepted standards. "She was a nonconformist who dressed, spoke, and lived differently from everyone around her."
  • Conformable (adjective) — capable of conforming; in agreement with. "His findings were conformable with the accepted theory."
  • Conformation (noun) — the shape or structure of something; how something is formed or arranged. (Note: this is slightly different — it refers to physical shape or molecular structure, not the act of conforming.) "The conformation of the protein determines its function."
  • Nonconformity (noun) — a failure or refusal to conform. "The product was rejected due to nonconformity with quality standards."

Social: She struggled to conform to her family's traditional expectations and eventually moved to a new city to live on her own terms.

Legal/Regulatory: All electrical appliances sold in this country must conform to national safety regulations.

Scientific: The new data conforms to the predictions made by the model.

Religious: Members of the sect were expected to conform to strict rules about diet and dress.

Architectural: The design of the new museum was created to conform to the surrounding historical landscape.

Workplace: Employees are expected to conform to the company's code of conduct at all times.

To conform is to align yourself, your behavior, or a thing with an existing rule, standard, pattern, or expectation — adjusting to fit what is required or expected, whether by society, an authority, or a formal specification.

If you ever see "conform" in a sentence, ask yourself: Who or what is adjusting? And what are they adjusting to match? The answer to those two questions will always unlock the meaning.
3274:
Conformation means the shape or structural arrangement of something — how its parts are put together and organized in space.

Think of it this way: if you took all the pieces of something and asked, "How are these pieces arranged relative to each other? What form does this thing take?", the answer to that question is its conformation.

These two words look and sound similar, but mean completely different things. This is one of the most common mix-ups in English.

  • Confirmation = verifying that something is true. "I received a confirmation that my order was placed."
  • Conformation = the shape or structure of something. "The conformation of the molecule determines how it behaves."

Remember: conformation is always about form and shape. In fact, you can see the word "form" hiding inside "conformation" — that's a useful memory trick.

In its broadest sense, conformation refers to the way something is shaped or put together. It describes the physical structure of an object, a body, or a system — specifically, how its individual parts are arranged in relation to one another.

For example, if someone says a building has an unusual conformation, they mean its structure or layout is unusual — the way the rooms, floors, and walls are arranged gives it a distinctive form.

This is where the word is most commonly used in everyday life outside of chemistry.

When people talk about the conformation of an animal — especially a horse, a dog, or livestock — they mean the physical structure and proportions of that animal's body. Are its legs straight and well-set? Is its back the right length? Are its muscles properly developed? Is everything in balance and proportion?

A horse with good conformation has a body structure that is well-suited for athletic performance: the legs are correctly angled, the spine is strong, the neck connects well to the shoulder, and so on. A horse with poor conformation might have legs that are poorly angled, which could make it prone to injury or less efficient at moving.

In dog shows, judges evaluate a dog's conformation against the official standard for that breed. This is literally called a conformation show — it's a competition to judge how closely a dog's physical structure matches the ideal blueprint for its breed.

So in biology, conformation is essentially: does this creature's body have the right shape and proportions?

This is where the word becomes especially precise and significant.

In chemistry, conformation refers to the specific three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule at any given moment, achieved by rotating around chemical bonds — without breaking any bonds.

Here's a simple mental model: imagine a molecule like a set of beads connected by flexible strings. You can twist and rotate the strings to change the shape of the whole structure without cutting any of the strings. Each different three-dimensional shape you can achieve through this twisting and rotating is a different conformation of that molecule. These different shapes are called conformers or conformational isomers.

A classic example: think of a simple chain of four carbon atoms. If you hold one end still and rotate the other end, the whole chain can be stretched out straight, or it can be bent into different angles. Each position — each distinct spatial arrangement — is a conformation.

Why does this matter? Because the conformation a molecule takes directly affects how it behaves, what it can interact with, and whether it is stable. In a crowded molecule, some conformations cause atoms to bump into each other (making that shape unstable), while other conformations spread the atoms out comfortably (making that shape stable and preferred). Molecules naturally tend to spend more time in their most stable conformations.

Proteins are large, complex molecules made of chains of amino acids. The conformation of a protein — its precise three-dimensional folded shape — is everything. It is not an exaggeration to say that a protein's conformation is its function.

When a protein folds into the right conformation, it can act as an enzyme (a biological machine that speeds up chemical reactions), a structural support, a signal carrier, or a receptor. When a protein's conformation is wrong — either because it misfolded or because something changed its shape — it often can't do its job. Some serious diseases, like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and prion diseases (like mad cow disease), are directly caused by proteins taking on wrong conformations and accumulating harmfully in the body.

Biologists and chemists spend enormous effort studying protein conformations because understanding the shape of a protein is key to understanding — and potentially controlling — its behavior.

"Conformation" always revolves around one central idea — shape, structure, and spatial arrangement — but it is applied at very different scales:

  • At the scale of an animal's whole body, it describes physical proportions and build.
  • At the scale of a molecule, it describes the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms.
  • At the scale of a protein, it describes the precise fold that gives the protein its identity and function.

In all of these uses, the question being answered is the same: What shape is this thing in? How are its parts arranged?

If you ever need to decide whether to use "conformation" or "confirmation" in writing, ask yourself: Am I talking about shape/structure, or am I talking about verification/proof? If it's shape and structure, it's "conformation." If it's proof or verification, it's "confirmation."
3275:
A conformist is a person who follows the rules, beliefs, behaviors, and expectations of the group around them — without seriously questioning whether those things are right or wrong, good or bad. They do what is considered "normal" by their society, community, or social group, and they actively avoid standing out or going against the flow.

Think of it this way: imagine a river. Most fish swim in one direction — the direction the current takes them. A conformist is a fish that swims exactly where the current goes, without ever wondering why it's going that way, or whether a different direction might be better.

To understand "conformist," you first need to understand the idea of social norms. Social norms are the unwritten (and sometimes written) rules of a group — things like how to dress, what to believe, how to behave, what career to choose, what opinions to hold, and so on. Every society, culture, workplace, school, and friend group has its own norms.

A conformist is someone who obeys these norms closely and without resistance. They don't challenge the norm. They don't ask "why?" They simply fall in line with what everyone else is doing or thinking.

Imagine you're in a school where everyone wears branded sneakers, listens to the same popular music, and makes fun of anyone who reads books for fun.

  • A conformist in this school will buy those branded sneakers, listen to that same music, and pretend they don't enjoy reading — even if privately, they love books. They adjust their behavior to fit in.
  • A non-conformist, by contrast, would wear whatever shoes they like, listen to whatever music they enjoy, and openly carry a book — even if it makes them look "different."

The conformist's driving force is the desire (often unconscious) to belong, be accepted, and avoid standing out.

A conformist typically:

  • Prioritizes fitting in over expressing their true self.
  • Accepts popular opinion as their own opinion, often without scrutiny.
  • Avoids conflict or controversy, preferring to agree with the majority.
  • Follows trends, whether in fashion, lifestyle, politics, or belief.
  • Feels uncomfortable or anxious when asked to go against the crowd.
  • Looks to others for cues on how to think, feel, and act.

The key point here is this: a conformist doesn't necessarily agree with the group deep down — they may privately think differently — but they behave in the way the group expects, because the social cost of being different feels too high.
The Spectrum: Light to Heavy Conformism

Conformism isn't black and white. It exists on a spectrum.

  • Mild conformists simply follow everyday social conventions — greeting people politely, dressing appropriately for different occasions, following workplace norms. This is largely harmless and is actually necessary for society to function smoothly.
  • Moderate conformists go further — they adopt the political opinions, religious views, or lifestyle choices of their community largely because that's what's expected of them, not because they have thought it through independently.
  • Extreme conformists will go along with a group even when the group is doing something harmful or clearly wrong, purely to avoid being cast out or judged. This is the most dangerous form of conformism — history has shown that it can enable injustice, discrimination, and even atrocities, because individuals stop thinking for themselves and simply follow the crowd.
The Tone of the Word — Is It an Insult?

In most modern usage, calling someone a "conformist" carries a mildly negative or critical tone. It implies that the person lacks independent thought, courage, or originality. It suggests that they have traded their authentic self for social approval.

However, the word is not always used as a harsh insult. Sometimes it is used in a neutral, descriptive way — simply to describe someone who prefers tradition, stability, and social harmony over novelty or rebellion.

The negativity of the word really kicks in when conformism crosses into blind conformism — following the group without any critical thought whatsoever.

This is important to understand, because conformism doesn't come from stupidity or weakness — it comes from very natural, deeply human instincts:

  • Fear of rejection. Humans are social creatures. Being excluded from a group feels painful — even threatening — at a biological level.
  • Desire for belonging. Fitting in creates a sense of community, warmth, and safety.
  • Uncertainty. When people don't know what to think or do, they look at what others are doing and copy it — it feels like the safe and "correct" option.
  • Upbringing. People who were raised in environments that punished difference and rewarded obedience often grow into conformists.
  • Social pressure. When a group is very vocal and consistent about what's "acceptable," it becomes psychologically hard to resist, even for otherwise confident people.

Since these two words are often used together, it helps to understand the contrast:

ConformistDoes what the group does; values acceptance and fitting in
Non-conformistDoes what they individually believe is right or authentic; values independence, even at social cost

Neither is entirely "good" or "bad." A society full of pure conformists would stagnate — no innovation, no reform, no moral progress. But a society with zero conformism would be chaotic — no shared values, no cooperation, no community.

The ideal, which most thoughtful people aim for, is selective conformism — following norms that make sense, and thoughtfully rejecting the ones that don't.
How to Use the Word in a Sentence

• "He was such a conformist that he changed his entire opinion the moment he saw the rest of the room disagree with him."
  • "The company's culture rewarded conformists and made it hard for creative thinkers to thrive."
  • "She had been a quiet conformist her whole life, but eventually found the courage to live on her own terms."
  • "Not every conformist is weak — sometimes choosing your battles and fitting in is simply practical."

A conformist is a person who shapes their behavior, beliefs, and lifestyle to match what their social group considers normal and acceptable — often at the expense of their own independent thinking or authentic self.
3276:
Conformity means going along with something — matching it, agreeing with it, or fitting into it. That "something" could be a rule, a standard, a norm, an expectation, or what a group of people does or believes.

Conformity is about alignment. When two things are in conformity, they are in agreement with each other. When a person is in conformity, they are in agreement with something outside themselves.
The Two Main Worlds This Word Lives In

The word "conformity" is used in two broad situations, and understanding both is key.

1. Social Conformity — Going Along with People and Groups

This is the most common use of the word in everyday life. Social conformity means changing or adjusting your behavior, opinions, or appearance to match what a group, society, or culture expects of you.

Humans are social creatures. From the day we are born, we are surrounded by unwritten (and written) rules about how to behave — how to dress, how to speak, what to believe, what to value. When people follow these rules — especially because others around them do — that is conformity.

Think of it this way: imagine you move to a new school. You notice everyone dresses a certain way, uses certain phrases, and behaves in a certain manner. If you start dressing the same way and adopting those habits to fit in, you are engaging in conformity. You are shaping yourself to match the group.

Conformity in this sense can be:

Conscious or unconscious. Sometimes people are fully aware they are conforming ("I'll just agree so no one argues with me"). Other times, it happens naturally without thinking — you simply absorb the norms of the people around you.

Voluntary or pressured. You might conform because you genuinely agree with the group. Or you might conform because you feel social pressure — fear of rejection, embarrassment, or punishment if you don't.

Outward or inward. Sometimes a person acts in line with the group (outward conformity) but doesn't personally believe in what they're doing. Other times, the person truly changes their inner beliefs to match the group (inward conformity, sometimes called "true" conformity).

2. Formal/Technical Conformity — Meeting a Standard or Rule

Outside of social situations, conformity is used to describe whether something meets a required standard, rule, or specification.

For example:

  • A product is in conformity with safety regulations if it meets all the required safety standards.
  • A building is in conformity with the law if it follows all the legal construction rules.
  • A student's essay is in conformity with the guidelines if it follows the format the teacher required.

In this sense, conformity has nothing to do with people following social pressure. It simply means compliance — something matches what it is supposed to match. It's a neutral, factual statement: either it conforms, or it doesn't.
Is Conformity a Good Thing or a Bad Thing?

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: conformity is not automatically good or bad. It depends entirely on the context.

When conformity is positive or necessary:
Following traffic laws is conformity — and it keeps everyone safe. Employees following workplace safety procedures are conforming to rules that protect lives. Children learning to say "please" and "thank you" are conforming to social norms that help society function smoothly. In these cases, conformity is healthy, helpful, and even essential.

When conformity is neutral:
Fashion trends, social rituals, or shared cultural habits — like the way people greet each other in a particular country — are forms of conformity that are neither harmful nor particularly meaningful. They simply reflect how groups coordinate their behavior.

When conformity is negative or harmful:
Conformity becomes problematic when it requires people to suppress their individuality, silence their conscience, or participate in something wrong just because "everyone else is doing it." History is filled with examples of groups committing terrible acts because individuals conformed to peer pressure or authority rather than acting on their own moral judgment. Social psychologist Solomon Asch famously demonstrated in his experiments that people will even deny the evidence of their own eyes — giving a clearly wrong answer — just to conform to what the group says.

Conformity can also stifle creativity and progress. Many great ideas, discoveries, and social reforms came from people who refused to conform.
The Spectrum: How Much Do People Conform?

People don't conform equally. There is a spectrum.

On one end, you have total conformity — someone who does exactly what the group expects, never questions norms, and fully molds their behavior and beliefs to fit in.

In the middle, you have selective conformity — most people live here. They conform in some areas of life (following laws, workplace norms, social etiquette) while asserting their individuality in others (personal beliefs, creative choices, lifestyle).

On the other end, you have nonconformity — the deliberate rejection of social norms and expectations. A nonconformist actively resists going along with the crowd and insists on their own way of thinking and living.
Why Does Conformity Happen? (The Psychology Behind It)

Understanding why people conform helps lock in the meaning of the word.

Belonging: Humans have a deep need to feel accepted. Conforming to a group's norms is often the easiest way to belong. The fear of being excluded or ridiculed is a powerful driver of conformity.

Uncertainty: When people don't know what to do in a situation, they look to others for guidance and copy their behavior. This is called informational conformity — you conform because you assume others know better.

Approval: People generally want to be liked and respected. Conforming to what others expect is a way of seeking their approval.

Avoiding conflict: It is often easier to go along with something than to challenge it, even if you privately disagree.

Knowing the family of words around "conformity" will make your understanding even stronger.

Conform (verb) — the action. "She chose to conform to the group's dress code."

Conformist (noun/adjective) — a person who conforms, especially one who follows norms very closely. "He was a conformist who never questioned the rules."

Nonconformity (noun) — the opposite of conformity; the refusal to follow expected norms. "Her nonconformity made her stand out from the crowd."

Nonconformist (noun) — a person who does not conform. "The artist was a well-known nonconformist who rejected mainstream culture."

Conformance (noun) — a more technical/formal synonym for conformity, especially used in business, law, and engineering. "The product passed the conformance test."
A Simple Summary to Tie It All Together

Conformity is the state of matching, fitting in with, or going along with something — whether that is a social group, a cultural norm, a rule, or a standard. In social life, it means adjusting your behavior or beliefs to align with those of others around you. In formal contexts, it means meeting a required standard or rule. It is driven by human needs for belonging, approval, and certainty. It can be beneficial when it holds society together and maintains order, and harmful when it overrides individual conscience or enables wrongdoing. Its opposite is nonconformity — the refusal to go along.
3277: "Confound" means to throw something into disorder — it can throw your understanding into disorder (leaving you baffled), throw your expectations into disorder (proving them wrong), or throw the distinction between two things into disorder by blurring them together. It always carries a sense of something being disrupted, defeated, or tangled.
Meaning 1: To completely baffle or bewilder someone

This is the most common meaning in modern usage. When something confounds you, it leaves you utterly stumped — you cannot explain it, cannot make sense of it, and are genuinely surprised by it. It is stronger than simply "confusing" you. It implies that the thing has, in a sense, defeated your ability to understand.

Examples:

  • "The patient's rapid recovery confounded the doctors." (The recovery was so unexpected that the doctors simply couldn't explain it.)
  • "His behavior confounds me — I cannot figure out why he acts this way."
  • "The complexity of the universe confounds even the greatest scientists."

Notice that the thing doing the confounding is usually something deeply unexpected or beyond normal explanation. The person who is confounded is left speechless or helpless in their attempt to understand.
Meaning 2: To mix up two different things — treating them as the same

When you confound two things, you fail to tell them apart. You treat thing A as if it is thing B, collapsing a distinction that should exist. Think of it as: the line between two separate things gets blurred and erased.

Examples:

  • "People often confound 'bravery' with 'recklessness' — but they are very different things."
  • "He confounded his personal opinions with objective facts."
  • "Don't confound love with obsession."

This meaning appears most often in careful, formal writing — in philosophy, science, and logic — wherever making precise distinctions matters a great deal. The warning "don't confound X with Y" means: "These two things may look or feel similar, but they are actually different — treat them as different."
Meaning 3: To defeat or prove wrong — especially expectations, predictions, or plans

When someone or something confounds an expectation or prediction, it acts in a way that makes that expectation completely wrong. The outcome is the opposite of what was anticipated. There is a strong sense of overturning something.

Examples:

  • "The young athlete confounded all predictions by winning the gold medal." (Nobody believed she would win — she did, and every prediction was proved wrong.)
  • "The new treatment confounded the skeptics by actually working."
  • "The general confounded his enemies' plans with a surprise attack."

This meaning often carries a triumphant or even satisfying tone. The thing that gets confounded is typically a negative or dismissive expectation — doubt, criticism, a pessimistic forecast — and confounding it means those doubters were proven wrong.
Meaning 4: To make something more complicated or difficult to analyze

In more formal and academic settings — especially science and research — "confound" means to introduce interference or complication into something, making it harder to understand clearly or draw clean conclusions from.

Examples:

  • "Several unexpected variables confounded the results of the experiment." (The variables muddied the results, making them hard to interpret.)
  • "The investigation was confounded by new, contradictory evidence."
  • "Poor weather confounded the rescue mission."

This is where the related term "confounding variable" (also called a "confounding factor") comes from — a hidden or uncontrolled element in an experiment that interferes with your results and makes it hard to know what is actually causing what. For example: if you're studying whether coffee improves focus, but your test subjects also sleep differently from each other, their sleep habits are a confounding variable — they "confound" your results.

These two words are related but not identical.

"Confuse" is broader and milder. You can be confused by simple things — unclear directions, a new concept, an unfamiliar word. Confusion is ordinary and everyday.

"Confound" is stronger and more intense. It implies a deeper, more total bafflement — the kind that genuinely stumps you, often because something is so unexpected or seemingly impossible to explain. It also carries the specific senses of mixing up two things and defeating expectations, which "confuse" does not.

A simple way to think about it: everything that confounds you also confuses you — but not everything that confuses you confounds you.

Synonyms by meaning:

  • Baffled, bewildered, stumped, perplexed, mystified (for the "baffle" sense)
  • Conflate, mix up, blur (for the "treat as the same" sense)
  • Foil, thwart, defeat, disprove (for the "prove wrong" sense)
  • Complicate, muddle, muddy (for the "make complex" sense)
A note on "confounded" as an old expression

You will sometimes see "confounded" used as an old-fashioned exclamation of frustration, similar to "damned" or "blasted":

  • "That confounded machine broke again!"
  • "Confound it!" (meaning roughly: "Damn it!")

This is informal, largely British, and old-fashioned — you will encounter it in classic novels and older films. You are unlikely to need to use it yourself, but now you will not be surprised when you see it.
The one thread that ties everything together

No matter which meaning you encounter, "confound" always involves something being disrupted or defeated:

  • It defeats your understanding → you are baffled.
  • It defeats the boundary between two things → they get mixed up.
  • It defeats an expectation or plan → it proves predictions wrong.
  • It defeats clarity in a situation → things become more complicated.

Once you see that common thread — disruption, defeat, disorder — the word will feel natural in all its forms, no matter the context.
3278: "Confounded" as an adjective actually carries two different meanings, and they feel quite different from each other. Both are correct. You need to know both to truly understand this word.

This is the more common and widely used meaning.

When someone is confounded, they are so deeply confused that they are almost frozen — unable to think clearly, respond quickly, or make sense of what is happening. It goes beyond just being "a little puzzled." It suggests a kind of mental paralysis, where something has genuinely thrown your mind into disarray.

Think of it this way: imagine a math professor who suddenly sees a calculation that completely contradicts everything she knows. She stares at it, mouth slightly open, unable to explain it. She is confounded.

What makes something "confound" you?

It is usually something:

  • Unexpected — it catches you completely off guard
  • Contradictory — it goes against what you believed to be true
  • Complex — it is too tangled or strange for your mind to quickly process

Examples in sentences:

  • "The detective was confounded by the case — the evidence made no sense at all."
  • "She gave him a confounded look when he said he had never heard of the internet."
  • "The scientist was confounded by the results, which contradicted three years of his research."

Synonyms (words with a very similar meaning):

Baffled, bewildered, stumped, flummoxed, perplexed, dumbfounded.

Subtle note: "Confounded" tends to suggest a slightly stronger sense of being thrown off than just "confused." Being confused might mean you need a moment to think. Being confounded often means you genuinely don't know where to even begin.
Meaning 2: A Mild, Old-Fashioned Expression of Annoyance

This meaning is very different from the first. Here, "confounded" is not really describing a person's mental state — it is being used as an intensifier, almost like a polite curse word, placed in front of a noun to express strong irritation or frustration about something.

It is the equivalent of saying "damned," "blasted," or "wretched" — but softer, more old-fashioned, and far more acceptable in polite or formal speech.

Think of it like this:

If someone is furious that their umbrella broke in the rain, they might yell: "This confounded umbrella!"
They don't mean the umbrella is confused. They mean: "This infuriating, annoying, wretched umbrella!"

This usage appears a lot in:

  • Classic British literature
  • Period dramas and old films
  • Formal or older writing where swearing was considered impolite

Examples in sentences:

  • "Where are my confounded keys? I've been searching for an hour!"
  • "That confounded dog dug up my garden again!"
  • "I cannot get this confounded machine to work!"

Why use "confounded" instead of just saying "annoying"?

Because it does more than label something as annoying — it vents emotion. It shows that the speaker has reached a point of genuine exasperation. "Annoying" is a calm, observational label. "Confounded" is an emotional outburst dressed in polite clothing.
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

The context always makes it clear:

  • If "confounded" describes a person or their expression, it almost certainly means baffled/bewildered.
    • "He had a confounded look on his face." → He looked totally lost and confused.
  • If "confounded" appears right before a thing (like a noun — a machine, a dog, a problem), and the tone is one of frustration, it is almost certainly the intensifier.
    • "This confounded machine!" → This maddening, infuriating machine!
A Note on Tone and Register

Both meanings carry a slightly formal or old-fashioned flavor. In casual, everyday modern speech, people are more likely to say "baffled" or "confused" instead of meaning 1, and "damned" or "bloody" (in British English) instead of meaning 2. However, "confounded" (especially meaning 1) still appears regularly in modern writing, journalism, and formal speech — and understanding it is essential for reading classic literature.
The One-Line Summary for Each Meaning

• Meaning 1: So confused and bewildered that you cannot easily think or respond. (A state of the mind.)
  • Meaning 2: A polite but emphatic way of expressing that something is extremely irritating or frustrating. (An emotional label placed on things.)

Master these two, and you have fully understood "confounded" as an adjective — in every context you will ever encounter it.
3279:
At the heart of "confront" is one powerful image: standing face-to-face with something you will not run away from. Whether it's a person, a problem, a fear, or an uncomfortable truth, to confront something means to face it directly, boldly, and without flinching.

The defining quality of "confront" is directness. It is the opposite of avoiding, ignoring, or going around something. It means you turn toward it, not away from it.
The Four Main Ways "Confront" Is Used

1. Facing a person directly to address a difficult issue

This is the most everyday use. When you confront someone, you approach them directly — usually to accuse them of something, question their behavior, or raise a difficult matter you can no longer ignore.

  • "She confronted her roommate about the missing money."
  • "He confronted his boss about the unfair treatment."
  • "The angry customer confronted the store manager."

Confronting someone doesn't always mean a screaming fight — but there is always a serious tension present. The key is that you go directly to that person. You're not hinting, not complaining to others behind their back, not dropping subtle signals. You walk up to them and say it to their face.

Sentence pattern: confront + someone + about + something

2. Facing a difficult situation, problem, truth, or emotion

Here, the thing you're confronting is not a person — it's a challenge, a crisis, a fear, or a reality. This is extremely common in serious, reflective, or formal writing.

  • "The country must confront its history of discrimination."
  • "He finally confronted his drinking problem."
  • "She confronted the fact that the relationship was over."
  • "You cannot solve a problem you refuse to confront."

This use carries a deep sense of courage and honesty. When you confront a difficult reality, you stop pretending it doesn't exist. You stop looking away. You turn toward it and deal with it honestly. This is often considered a brave and mature thing to do.

Sentence pattern: confront + a problem / fear / truth / reality

3. When something difficult suddenly appears in front of you

In this use, you are not the one doing the confronting — something is confronting you. This form is almost always passive: "be confronted with" or "be confronted by."

  • "When she walked into the office, she was confronted by an angry crowd."
  • "He opened the report and was immediately confronted with devastating news."
  • "The rescuers were confronted with a scene of total destruction."
  • "Every morning, she was confronted by the same impossible choice."

Here, something difficult, shocking, or overwhelming appears right in front of you — often suddenly, often without warning — and you have no choice but to deal with it.

Sentence pattern: be confronted with/by + something

A small but useful note: "confronted by" often feels like a person or a force is facing you head-on, while "confronted with" often suggests a fact, situation, or piece of information is being placed in front of you. In real life, the two prepositions are used somewhat interchangeably, and both are correct in most situations.

4. Presenting someone with evidence, facts, or an uncomfortable truth

In this sense, one person places something — usually evidence, a contradiction, or a hard fact — directly in front of another person, often to challenge or expose them.

  • "The detective confronted the suspect with the security footage."
  • "The journalist confronted the politician with his own earlier statements."
  • "Her therapist confronted her with the self-destructive patterns in her behavior."

This is similar to Sense 1 (facing a person directly), but here there is a specific piece of information being used as the confronting tool. The structure is: you confront a person with information.

Sentence pattern: confront + someone + with + something (evidence / facts / truth)

"Confront" is not a neutral word. It always carries a feeling of difficulty, courage, or tension. You confront things that are uncomfortable, threatening, painful, or challenging — things that you (or someone else) have been trying to avoid.

You would never naturally say "I confronted my favorite song" or "she confronted a beautiful sunset" — because those things are not difficult to face. The word only makes sense where there is something hard, serious, or charged involved. If the thing being faced isn't difficult in some way, "confront" is the wrong word.

This also means that "confront" often implies courage. When someone confronts a bully, confronts their addiction, or confronts an injustice, we understand that they did something that took bravery — because the easier thing would have been to walk away.

Confront vs. Face
"Face" is a lighter, more neutral word. You can face something pleasant or unpleasant. "Confront" is heavier — it always implies something difficult, and it carries a stronger sense of deliberate boldness.

  • "She faced the camera." → neutral; she simply turned toward it
  • "She confronted her fear of cameras." → bold, effortful, emotionally charged

Confront vs. Address
"Address" is more formal and calm — it means to deal with or speak about something in a measured way. "Confront" is more intense — it implies a sharper directness and often a higher emotional charge.

  • "The mayor addressed concerns about crime." → professional, composed
  • "The mayor confronted critics directly." → bolder, more charged, more head-on

Confront vs. Tackle
"Tackle" focuses on solving or working through a problem actively. "Confront" focuses on the act of facing it — the willingness to look at it squarely. You might confront a fear first, and then tackle it.

  • "She confronted her anxiety." → she acknowledged it and faced it honestly
  • "She tackled her anxiety." → she worked hard to overcome it

There is also a meaningful reflexive use of this word — when you turn the confrontation inward. To confront yourself (or confront oneself) means to honestly face your own flaws, mistakes, biases, or uncomfortable truths about who you are.

  • "After years of blaming others, he finally confronted himself and accepted responsibility."

This is considered one of the most difficult and important things a person can do — and the word "confront" captures that weight perfectly.

"Confront" always involves two things: directness and difficulty. Whether you're standing face-to-face with a person to address something hard, facing a serious problem in your own life, being suddenly met with a shocking situation, or placing uncomfortable evidence in front of someone — the word always signals the same thing: no more avoiding, no more going around it. We are facing this now, directly and honestly.
